headline: Most Americans say no to AI data centers in their towns

sources.title: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers
Americans Oppose AI Data Centers in Their Area
Michigan town erupts over proposed AI data center as fight gets political (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: Across the United States, huge AI [[data centers]] are {{springing up}} near small towns, and many residents are {{pushing back}}. A Gallup poll {{carried out}} in March found that 71 percent of Americans oppose building a data center in their area. Almost half, 48 percent, are strongly against the idea. Only 27 percent are [[in favor]]. Opposition is strongest in the Midwest, at 76 percent, and weakest in the West, at 63 percent.

verbs.correct: To appear suddenly in many places
verbs.wrong: To start a company or organization
verbs.why: Coffee shops spring up on every corner of a busy street, and new apps spring up every month. The story says AI data centers are springing up near small towns across the United States.

verbs.correct: To resist or oppose a plan
verbs.wrong: To hire extra workers for a job
verbs.why: Employees push back when a manager wants weekend work, and parents push back against a longer school day. Many residents are pushing back against data centers in their towns.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.wrong: To keep something for a later time
verbs.why: A mechanic carries out a full check of the car, and a school carries out a fire drill every year. Gallup carried out its poll in March and published it in May.

chunks.text: Why do so many people say no? Half of the [[opponents]] {{bring up}} resource use. Data centers {{eat up}} enormous amounts of electricity and water. Another 22 percent worry about [[quality of life]], and 20 percent fear the cost effects. Fifteen percent expect their own [[utility bills]] to {{go up}}. The [[supporters]] {{weigh up}} the same project differently. Two thirds of them say a data center would help the [[local economy]], and 55 percent expect new jobs.

verbs.correct: To mention a topic in a discussion
verbs.why: A student brings up a question at the end of class, and a friend brings up an old story at dinner. Half of the opponents bring up resource use when they explain their objections.

verbs.correct: To use a very large amount of something
verbs.wrong: To supply a town with water and power
verbs.why: Video calls eat up a phone's battery, and a long commute eats up two hours of the day. Data centers eat up enormous amounts of electricity and water.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher level or price
verbs.why: Rent goes up every year in big cities, and the temperature goes up in the afternoon. Fifteen percent of opponents expect their own utility bills to go up.
A buyer weighs up two used cars before choosing, and a student weighs up a job offer against more study. Supporters weigh up the same project and see the local economy first.

chunks.text: The opposition has real effects. In 2025, local [[resistance]] delayed or canceled projects worth 156 billion dollars. In Indiana, one company {{gave up}} a 1.3 billion dollar project after the town council opposed it. In Virginia, a [[planning commission]] {{turned down}} a 12 billion dollar project with a [[unanimous]] vote. In Arizona, a [[developer]] {{pulled out}} of a 14 billion dollar plan after officials blocked a [[rezoning]]. In July alone, residents {{turned out}} for 142 protests across 42 states.

verbs.correct: To stop a plan and not try again
verbs.wrong: To hand something to many people
verbs.why: A runner gives up a race after an injury, and a family gives up the idea of moving abroad. One company gave up a 1.3 billion dollar project in Indiana after the town council opposed it.

verbs.correct: To refuse a request or an offer
verbs.wrong: To give control to someone else
verbs.why: A bank turns down a loan request, and a singer turns down an invitation to a festival. A planning commission in Virginia turned down a 12 billion dollar project.

verbs.correct: To leave a plan or an agreement
verbs.wrong: To attract money or new business
verbs.why: A sponsor pulls out of a tournament, and a buyer pulls out of a house deal at the last minute. In Arizona, a developer pulled out of a 14 billion dollar plan.

verbs.correct: To go somewhere to join an event
verbs.wrong: To refuse to let someone enter
verbs.why: Thousands of fans turn out for a parade, and neighbors turn out for a street cleanup. Residents turned out for 142 protests across 42 states in July.

chunks.text: Some state governments are now {{stepping in}}. On July 14, New York {{brought in}} the first [[statewide]] [[moratorium]]. It covers any [[facility]] that would use 50 [[megawatts]] or more. Texas announced its own pause on August 10. Maine's [[legislature]] passed a moratorium in April, but the state's governor [[vetoed]] it. The industry still promises jobs and [[tax revenue]]. Yet residents keep {{speaking out}}, and the fight is far from over.

verbs.correct: To take action in a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To leave a top job or position
verbs.why: A teacher steps in when two students start fighting, and a referee steps in to stop a rough game. Some state governments are stepping in with rules on new data centers.

verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule or law
verbs.wrong: To make a price or level lower
verbs.why: A city brings in a ban on smoking in parks, and a school brings in a new dress code. New York brought in the first statewide moratorium on July 14.

verbs.correct: To say your opinion in public
verbs.wrong: To talk on behalf of a group
verbs.why: Nurses speak out about long shifts, and a former player speaks out against a coach. Residents across the country keep speaking out against new data centers.

mainIdea.s: Most Americans oppose AI data centers near their homes, and local resistance is stopping big projects. Some states have now paused new facilities.
mainIdea.why: A Gallup poll found 71 percent against, local opposition delayed or canceled 156 billion dollars of projects in 2025, and New York and Texas announced moratoriums.

mainIdea.s: Most Americans support AI data centers because of jobs, but a few towns are pushing back. New York has banned them permanently across the state.
mainIdea.why: Close, but 71 percent of Americans oppose a data center in their area, and New York's moratorium is a pause that covers only facilities using 50 megawatts or more.

mainIdea.s: A power company raised utility bills across the Midwest to pay for new AI data centers. Residents in three states are now suing the company in court.
mainIdea.why: The story is about a poll, local protests and state moratoriums, not a lawsuit against a power company.

tf.s: A Gallup poll found that 71 percent of Americans oppose a data center in their area.
tf.why: The poll, carried out in March, found 71 percent against, and 48 percent strongly against.

tf.s: Half of the opponents bring up quality of life as their main concern.
tf.why: Half of the opponents bring up resource use, and only 22 percent mention quality of life.

tf.s: In Virginia, a planning commission turned down a 12 billion dollar project.
tf.why: The commission turned it down with a unanimous vote, and the project was delayed.

tf.s: In Arizona, a developer pulled out of a 1.3 billion dollar plan.
tf.why: The developer in Arizona pulled out of a 14 billion dollar plan, and the 1.3 billion dollar project was in Indiana.

tf.s: New York brought in the first statewide moratorium on July 14.
tf.why: It covers any facility that would use 50 megawatts or more, and Texas announced its own pause on August 10.

tf.s: Maine's governor signed the moratorium that the legislature passed in April.
tf.why: The state's governor vetoed the moratorium, so Maine has not stepped in the way New York did.
